entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Notion__notion-search
entries.description:
Search Notion pages and databases, or look up a user by name or email. Does not search connected apps; use connector_search, when listed, for sources such as Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, mail, or calendar. When connector_search is listed, call it in parallel with search on the first search for an information need, unless the user names a source, the request is a user lookup, or the request is about Notion pages or databases themselves, such as finding a page to read or edit. Decisions, status updates, and discussions often live in connected sources. Preserve distinctive names and identifiers.

Use a non-empty query for content searches. Leave the query empty only when you also send filters or a non-relevance sort, as in the browse example below. Omit optional parameters unless needed. Do not add filters or sorting just to fill in defaults. Business or Enterprise is required for filters.edited_by_user_ids, filters.last_edited_date_range, filters.title_only=true, filters.content_status, more than one distinct teamspace across teamspace_id and filters.teamspace_ids, and sort other than relevance. On other plans, those options are dropped with a notice in the result, and results may be broader. Keep filters nested inside "filters". Use YYYY-MM-DD for start_date and end_date. Use page_size, not limit.

For user lookup, set query_type="user" and provide a name or email. A document about a person is a content search, not a user lookup.

<example description="Find a page by title">
{"query":"Q3 roadmap"}
</example>
<example description="Browse pages you edited most recently">
{"query":"","filters":{"edited_by_user_ids":["me"]},"sort":"last_edited"}
</example>
<example description="Find a user">
{"query":"alex@example.com","query_type":"user"}
</example>

query.description: Short, specific keywords for Notion content search. For user search, enter a name or email address. Provide a non-empty query unless intentionally browsing with filters or a non-relevance sort.

query_type.description: Specify type of the query as either "internal" or "user". Always include this input if performing "user" search.

data_source_url.description: Optionally restrict keyword search to a data source URL returned in a <data-source> tag.

page_url.description: Optionally restrict keyword search to a page and its descendants. Accepts a Notion page URL or ID.

teamspace_id.description: Optionally, provide the ID of a teamspace to restrict search results to. This will perform a search over content within the specified teamspace only. Accepts the teamspace ID (UUIDv4) with or without dashes.

filters.description: Optional exact filters for Notion workspace search. Omit unless required by the request. Keep filter fields nested here; do not send them at the top level. Some filters require Business access.

created_date_range.description: Optional filter to only produce search results created within the specified date range.

start_date.description: The start date of the date range as an ISO 8601 date string, if any.

end_date.description: The end date of the date range as an ISO 8601 date string, if any.

created_by_user_ids.description: Optional filter to only produce search results created by the Notion users that have the specified user IDs. Use "me" for the connected user.

edited_by_user_ids.description: Optional filter to only produce search results edited by the Notion users that have the specified user IDs. Use "me" for the connected user. Available on the Business plan.

last_edited_date_range.description: Optional filter to only produce search results last edited within the specified date range. Available on the Business plan.

start_date.description: The start date of the date range as an ISO 8601 date string, if any.

end_date.description: The end date of the date range as an ISO 8601 date string, if any.

teamspace_ids.description: Optional filter to only produce search results inside one of the specified teamspaces. Selecting more than one teamspace is available on the Business plan; use teamspace_id for one teamspace on other plans.

title_only.description: When true, match the query only against page and database titles instead of page content. Available on the Business plan.

content_status.description: Which pages to include by status. Omit for the default live pages. Supplying this field, even with the default value, requires Business access.

sort.description: Result ordering for Notion workspace search. Omit for the default "relevance" ordering. "last_edited" and "created" require Business access.

page_size.description: Maximum number of results to return (default 10). Lower values reduce response size. Values outside the range (minimum 1, maximum 50) are clamped.

max_highlight_length.description: Maximum character length for result highlights (default 200). Set to 0 to omit highlights entirely. Values outside the range (minimum 0, maximum 500) are clamped.

instructions_version.description: Notion setup instructions version, such as 0.0.2. Omit if unknown.

skill.description: For tracking only: the name of the agent skill you are following for this task, such as notion-meeting-prep. Omit if you are not following a skill.

## Recommendations from "Building always-on agents"

**Event inbox**
- Route every event source (webhooks, schedules, background jobs, user messages) into a durable inbox rather than calling the agent directly. Direct calls can start competing runs and lose events on a crash.
- Use a database table that tracks each event's status and deduplicates by source identifiers.
- Keep the handler fast. Acknowledge events quickly, and defer deeper checks such as prompt-injection screening to the run.
- Treat the inbox as the source of truth. A replacement worker should re-read pending events, so a crashed run can be retried.
- Start with one inbox per user, and split it only if you need more parallelism.

**Single worker per inbox**
- Allow only one active worker per inbox to prevent duplicated work or overwritten changes.
- When an event arrives mid-run, choose one of three handling strategies: queue it for the next run, fold it into the current run, or interrupt and restart.

**Batching**
- Merge pending events into one run. If a user sends several messages in a row, the agent should reply once.

**Timers vs. inbox**
- Store timers separately from the inbox. The inbox should hold only events ready to be worked on.
- Follow-ups are deadlines the agent sets for itself, such as checking on a reply. Schedules are recurring tasks that also need to track their recurrence.
- Timers never start runs directly. A scheduler polls at a fixed interval and, for each due timer, marks follow-ups done, advances schedules to their next occurrence, and adds an event to the inbox.

**Session resume vs. fresh**
- Events that continue earlier work, such as a user reply, resume the existing session. Other events start a new session.
- A new session loads only the baseline overhead (system prompt, tools, memory) and the triggering event. A resumed session brings back its full prior transcript.
- Keep the baseline lean and use prompt caching to reduce costs.
- When a session grows too long, either compact older messages or start a new session. Both lose detail, so "anything that needs to persist should be saved to memory" beforehand.

**Mid-run events and deferral**
- While a deferred tool call waits for input, the run ends and the session is saved mid-call. The worker can process other events in the meantime, so the agent is not blocked.

**Memory**
- Store memory in its own durable store (a database or object store) so it outlives workers.
- Hold only what the agent cannot look up again. For information that lives in another system, store a pointer. "memory should only hold what the agent can't look up again" is the governing rule.
- Maintain four kinds of memory:
  - **User instructions:** a dedicated file, loaded at the start of every run.
  - **User notes:** learned preferences and corrections. Load an index and pull individual files on demand.
  - **Past messages:** a record of what has already been told to the user, to avoid repetition.
  - **Task progress:** a per-task file recording what is done and what remains.
- **Dreaming:** periodically review past sessions to curate memory. This can replace outdated entries and surface patterns that appear only across many runs.

**Permissions and deferral**
- For each tool call, the agent should proceed, block, or wait for approval.
- Auto mode uses classifiers to block dangerous actions, but "User review, however, is still necessary for the most important decisions."
- Deferred tool calls show the request to the user. Their answer returns as an inbox event that resumes the saved session in a new run.

**Credentials proxy**
- Keep credentials outside the agent's environment. The agent sends requests without them, and a proxy adds the real credentials before forwarding. The agent never holds the secrets.

**Outbox: notify vs. silent**
- A run ends in one of three ways: send a message, stay silent because nothing needs sending, or make a deferred request for permission or input.
- Most agents can use a direct "send" tool. Add a formal outbox (a table plus a dispatcher) only to pace messages or recover from delivery errors.
- Tune message volume with evals. Too many messages create noise, and too few miss important information. "start quiet and then earn more of the user's attention over time" is the recommended posture.

The lightweight discipline is simple: when a decision is non-trivial and someone might wonder later "why did we do it this way?", write it down here. ## Founding context The broad architectural decisions about repo topology, contracts, shared logic, and the open-core boundary are captured in [Polyglot Monorepo Scoping](https://www.notion.so/368830e8fbaa8101b0ffded7a3de3b53). ADRs that follow should reference and build on that document rather than relitigating it. ## Format Each ADR is its own sub-page under this one, using a lightweight MADR-style template. Title pattern: ADR-NNNN: Decision summary, where NNNN is a zero-padded sequential number. Each page should contain: - Status — proposed / accepted / superseded by ADR-XXXX / deprecated - Date — when the decision was accepted (ISO 8601) - Context — what's the situation that forces a decision? - Decision — what did we decide? - Consequences — what becomes easier, harder, or impossible because of this? - Alternatives considered — what else was on the table, and why was it not chosen? When a decision is later reversed, do not delete the original ADR. Mark its status as superseded by ADR-XXXX and write a new ADR that links back to it. The history is the point. ## When to write an ADR vs. update guidelines - ADR — a decision with trade-offs, alternatives, and consequences. Example: "Use Connect-ES 2.0 over grpc-web for the TS proto stack." - Guideline — a convention or rule the team follows. Example: "All Rust crates use cargo nextest for tests." If in doubt: did the choice have viable alternatives? If yes, it's an ADR. content.content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"ADR-0026: The gateway accepts DPoP-bound tokens (RFC 9449), and IAM checks the proof, off by default","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/3ef830e8fbaa81c6becff1905040b1f5?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ef830e8fbaa81c6becff1905040b1f5 as of 2026-10-04T08:10:44.533Z: {"title":"ADR-0026: The gateway accepts DPoP-bound tokens (RFC 9449), and IAM checks the proof, off by default"} {"type":"icon","icon":{"name":"rubber-stamp","color":"green"}} Status: Accepted (Sven approved the SMA-700 spec at GATE 1 on 2026-10-04) Date: 2026-10-04 Issue: SMA-700. Related: SMA-690. Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-04-sma-700-dpop-proof-check-design.md (paigasus-core) ## Context SMA-690 made IAM refuse every sender-constrained access token: a token with a cnf claim, or with a Keycloak payload typ of DPoP. IAM could not check the key binding. SMA-690 decision D11 recorded this with no ADR. The consequence is that a client that uses DPoP (RFC 9449) cannot use Paigasus. Keycloak 26.4 binds an access token when the client sends a DPoP header to the token endpoint. The realm needs no setting for this (SMA-690 measurement M2). A DPoP-bound token from Keycloak always has typ: DPoP and cnf.jkt. The chart gives no external route to IAM's own API: the ingress routes only to the consoles, and the IAM Service is ClusterIP. An API client reaches Paigasus through the Rust gateway, which the operator deploys. The gateway authenticates each request with two IAM calls: Introspect, then IsAuthorized, which authenticates with the client token. The gateway does not know its own public URL. ## Decision 1. The gateway accepts Authorization: DPoP with one DPoP proof header. It sends the proof, the method and the path to IAM in a new optional IntrospectRequest.dpop field. It skips the API-key leg for this scheme. 2. IAM checks the proof as RFC 9449 § 4.3 specifies: typ, alg (ES256, RS256), the jwk and the signature, htm, htu, the iat window, ath, the RFC 7638 thumbprint against cnf.jkt, and jti replay. 3. IAM checks htu against configured public base URLs of the gateway (forwarded_base_urls). A base URL can carry a path prefix that a proxy removes. Neither service builds a URL from Host or X-Forwarded-* headers. 4. IsAuthorized accepts a one-time follow-up: the gateway sends the same token and proof again, and IAM accepts them once, only for IsAuthorized, only while the replay entry of that exact proof is live. 5. The feature is off by default, with one switch in IAM and one in the gateway. 6. On the Bearer scheme, the SMA-690 refusal stays. IAM's own API keeps refusing the DPoP scheme. 7. The JOSE checks are an adapter behind a core port. The replay store is in memory, behind a ReplayStore port, with a global capacity and quotas for each key and each subject. A quota hit is a 429 with Retry-After at the gateway. A full global capacity fails closed with a retryable 503. 8. On the DPoP scheme, IAM checks the proof before any identity lookup or provisioning. The new error reason INVALID_DPOP_PROOF is in the shared range (909), because IAM and the gateway both emit it. 9. Server-provided nonces (RFC 9449 § 8) are out of scope. mTLS-bound tokens (RFC 8705) stay refused (SMA-690 D4). ## Consequences - A DPoP client can use the gateway when an operator turns the feature on in both services. A stolen DPoP-bound token is useless without the private key. - The in-memory replay store couples DPoP to the single IAM replica. A change to more than one replica must first add a shared store behind the same port. - A restart of IAM clears the replay store. A proof used before the restart can be used again until its iat window ends (at most 120 s with the defaults). - The operator must list the gateway's public URLs correctly. A wrong entry refuses DPoP requests; it does not accept a wrong one. - Introspect and the follow-up trust their in-cluster caller for the method and the path. The proof still needs the client's private key. - Each new ErrorReason value (INVALID_DPOP_PROOF) changes the TS and Rust error tables. ## Alternatives considered - Keep refusing bound tokens (SMA-690 status quo). Rejected: DPoP clients cannot use Paigasus. - Accept a bound token as a bearer token. Rejected for security (SMA-690 D10). - DPoP on IAM's own API. Rejected for now: the chart gives no route to it, and no shipped client calls it. - Derive htu from Host and X-Forwarded-*. Rejected: a client or a proxy controls these headers. - For the authz step: Introspect also authorizes. Rejected: the org resolution would move from the gateway into IAM. - For the authz step: the gateway authorizes as its own identity. Rejected: it reverses the self-query decision and needs a policy for the gateway identity. - A Redis replay store now. Rejected while IAM runs one replica; the port keeps this option open. - Server nonces (RFC 9449 § 8). Deferred: they need a challenge round trip and nonce state. content.content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"ADR-0027: Gateway tool-call interception — Cedar decisions in the gateway, Dogwood compiled in IAM, history in Redis","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/412830e8fbaa81dd8d46f14859edfb83?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/412830e8fbaa81dd8d46f14859edfb83 as of 2026-11-16T22:10:31.474Z: {"title":"ADR-0027: Gateway tool-call interception — Cedar decisions in the gateway, Dogwood compiled in IAM, history in Redis"} null Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-08 Decided by: Sven Maschek Issue: [SMA-747](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-747) Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-09-sma-749-tool-call-assembler-design.md (paigasus-core, SMA-749) Amended: 2026-11-09, decision (f), after the SMA-748 spike; 2026-11-16, decision (e), the gateway's IAM identity for the policy fetch (SMA-775), and decision (g), the longest window Builds on: ADR-0005, ADR-0012, ADR-0013, ADR-0019, ADR-0025 ## Context The gateway proxies chat requests, but it does not understand tools. It cannot see which tool the model wants to call, with which arguments, or what a tool returned. So it cannot stop an agent from calling a tool it should not call. We want two kinds of protection: - Governance. A tenant decides which tools each org, team or key may call, and with which arguments. - Defence against injected or rogue agents. A tool result can carry a prompt injection. An agent can try to send data out or escape its sandbox. Some rules need history, not one request. Example: "no outbound email after a secret was read in the same session". The Notion "AI Gateway" scoping page planned for this. Section 6.6 defines a Guardrail hook chain at the request, the response and each stream chunk. Section 11 lists two ADRs that must come first: the guardrail interface, and the canonical model including tool calls. Neither was written. The hook chain was never built. The same page has two rules this decision must change: - The v1 non-goals exclude "tool-calling routing logic". - The performance target says "streaming first-token passthrough with no added buffering". A tool call cannot be checked before its arguments are complete. We compared three existing designs (research on 2026-11-08): - LiteLLM. Python guardrail hooks, a YAML tool permission guardrail, a tool policy registry, and MCP permissions. Enforcement depends on the route. Some endpoints skip it (issues #30732 and #32201). Its tool permission guardrail buffers the whole stream. Its exact-match blocklist could be bypassed with a change of case or a trailing space. - Hugging Face safeagents. A local proxy in front of a coding agent. It streams text and holds only tool calls until they are complete. Then it allows the call or replaces it with a notice. Deterministic checks run first, then a scanner, then an optional judge model that can only add blocks. It does not inspect tool results. It trusts the conversation history that the client sends. - AWS Dogwood and AgentCore Policy. AgentCore Policy evaluates Cedar at an agent tool gateway. It is deny by default and has a log-only mode. Dogwood (open source, Apache-2.0, Rust, August 2026) extends Cedar with when temporal clauses over the history of tool calls. Its lower step turns a policy into plain Cedar plus context slots that history fills. The reference interpreter is marked not for production. It keeps history in memory, does not check timestamps, and does not log decisions. Helikon already has an in-agent design: PermissionPolicy (Allow, Deny, AskUser, Replace), Guardrail and Hook. It is not connected to the gateway. ## Decision (a) The gateway checks tool calls at one point, after it reads them into a provider-neutral model. - The first version covers OpenAI Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages. Anthropic ingress is pulled forward from M2. - Each ingress has a converter into a ToolTurn: tool definitions, tool results, and earlier tool calls. - Every rule and every detector works on this model. A new ingress gets the same checks with no rule changes. This avoids the route-dependent gaps of LiteLLM. - The original bytes are kept. When nothing changes, they are forwarded unchanged. (b) Streaming holds only tool calls. - Text frames pass through at once. The time to the first text token does not change. - When a tool call starts, its frames and all later frames are held, in order, until the call is complete. - Each held call has a byte cap and a time cap. While a call is held, the gateway sends SSE keep-alive comments. - This decision replaces the PRD rule with: text is never held; a tool call's frames are held until the call is complete. (c) A blocked tool call is replaced by an assistant notice. The request does not fail. - OpenAI: the call's deltas are dropped and a delta.content notice is sent. The remaining calls are renumbered. If every call is blocked, finish_reason becomes stop. - Anthropic: the tool_use block becomes a text block at the same index. If every call is blocked, stop_reason becomes end_turn. - The decision is also sent as an SSE comment (: paigasus-decision), or as a paigasus-tool-decisions header when not streaming. - On the request side, the gateway can remove a tool definition, or replace a tool result with a notice. It never edits the text of a tool result. (d) Cedar decides. Tenants write the policies in IAM. - Each tenant has a tool catalog in IAM. Each tool becomes a Cedar action in the action group Action::"InvokeTool". A tool that is not in the catalog is evaluated as Action::"Unregistered", so Cedar's deny-by-default blocks it. - Tool names are normalised before matching: trim, Unicode NFC, then compare case-insensitively. - The context holds the arguments (context.input), the findings of the detectors, the request, the session and the history slots. - An operator floor is a platform policy set in IAM. It may contain only forbid policies. Cedar's rule that a forbid wins over any permit means a tenant cannot loosen it. - The modes are off, log-only and enforce. A tenant starts in log-only mode with an allow-everything starter policy. - Fail-open or fail-closed is an explicit setting. (e) The gateway evaluates. IAM does not get a call for each tool call. - The decision types and decide() live in paigasus-kernel. They are synchronous and pure, so Helikon can reuse them (ADR-0005). - The gateway caches each tenant's compiled policy set. An IAM change event clears the cached copy. A periodic refresh is a backstop. The gateway has one IAM credential, for the policy fetch only. (Amended 2026-11-16, SMA-775.) - The gateway fetches a tenant's compiled set after an IAM change event or on the refresh timer. No caller is present at that time, so the fetch cannot use a caller's key. - IAM has a new system role tool_policy_reader. It holds the action ReadCompiledToolPolicies and no other action. - A dedicated gateway service account holds this role at Root. IAM has no system service accounts, so an operator makes this account by hand, in a platform organization that the operator owns, and gives it an API key. The operator runbook describes the steps. - The gateway reads the account's credential from a file (iam.service_credential_file). It reads the file again when the file changes, so a rotation needs no restart. - The gateway sends this credential only on GetCompiledToolPolicies and GetCompiledFloorPolicies. It sends it on no other RPC. - The per-request self-query does not change. IsAuthorized still carries the caller's own key and asks about the caller's own principal (SMA-446, D9). The gateway credential cannot authorize a caller's request. - Alternative not chosen: grant the read action to gateway_user. Every API-key holder could then read the compiled policies of its organization. - Risk: a leaked gateway credential exposes every tenant's compiled tool policies, but no other data. The role has one action, and the credential can be rotated without a restart. (f) Dogwood is a front end in IAM, restricted to a fixed set of history shapes. It is not an interpreter in the gateway. (Amended 2026-11-09 after the SMA-748 spike: "A-restricted".) - When a tenant saves a policy, IAM validates it with Dogwood and runs lower. Dogwood runs in its own cargo workspace or binary inside IAM, because it pins cedar-policy 4.11 and cannot join rs/. - IAM translates each temporal block into a Paigasus-owned history-condition format. Only these shapes are accepted: formerly within W, count_within W with a comparison, sum_within W with a comparison, and possibly count_distinct_within. Any other shape, or a failed lowering, rejects the save. - IAM stores the source, the compiled Cedar, the translated conditions with stable slot names (lower_with_distincter), and the pinned Dogwood revision. IAM implements @scope per policy itself, because Dogwood applies its history partitioning to the whole policy set. - The gateway evaluates the conditions from its own history store, fills the slots, and evaluates plain Cedar. It matches Dogwood's semantics: a closed window \[now−W, now\], the current request counted toward count_within, and only request events decided. A missing slot fails closed. - A Dogwood bump does not change running policies. A re-compile job must run, and it reports any differences. - Why restricted: the spike (SMA-748, 2026-11-09) found that lowered Cedar validates and evaluates under cedar-policy 4.14, and matched dogwood replay on 14 of 14 decisions. But Dogwood exports no machine-readable slot format, cannot share the workspace's Cedar version, and needs a cargo deny exception for tiny-keccak. A fixed set of shapes gives tenants Dogwood syntax on top of a gateway evaluator we own. More shapes can be added later, one at a time. (g) The gateway keeps a trusted history in Redis. - Two event kinds: call (a tool call the model proposed, with a verdict) and result (a tool result the client claims). - Only the gateway clock sets timestamps. Each event is bound to the authenticated principal. - Requests are linked into a session by the tool call ids the gateway forwarded. A policy can also read the history of the principal or the key, with @scope("principal") or @scope("key"), so a client cannot escape a rule by starting a new conversation. - A call event is written as pending before the decision and updated afterwards. Concurrent requests therefore see each other. This is the reserve-then-charge pattern of ADR-0025. - Only the argument fields that policies use are stored, plus a hash of all arguments. Tool result content is never stored. - Limits: a longest window of 24 hours, and at most 10,000 events per history. (Amended 2026-11-16: Dogwood limits every window to 24 hours, so IAM refuses a longer window. The 7-day maximum is not available.) (h) Detectors produce findings. Only Cedar decides. - Built-in detectors: undeclared tool, name collision, invalid arguments, host not seen in the conversation, secret in arguments, injection markers in tool results, and history findings (forged history, mixed sessions, truncated history). - An optional judge model runs only on suspicious calls. It sees only the system and user messages, the call and the findings. It can add a block. It can never remove one. - A signed webhook lets external providers add findings. It cannot change content. (i) Every decision is logged as an event. - A new ToolDecisionEvent proto embeds AuditMetadata (ADR-0012). It holds no raw arguments or content. - Events go into a Redis stream first and are published to NATS JetStream. - A CLI exports the log in Dogwood's trace format, so a tenant can test a policy with dogwood replay before enforcing it. - New error codes go in a gateway block of error.proto (ADR-0019). (j) An MCP gateway is a later phase. It reuses the same action, history and decision log (SMA-756). ## Consequences Positive - One check point covers every ingress, so a new endpoint cannot skip the checks. - Text streaming keeps its latency. Only tool calls wait. - Tenants write policies in Cedar, which the platform already uses, and can use Dogwood sequence rules. - The not-for-production Dogwood interpreter never runs on live traffic. - Helikon can reuse the decision shape, so the agent side and the gateway side can enforce the same policy. - Log-only mode and trace replay let a tenant test a policy before it blocks anything. Negative and risks - The gateway no longer forwards bytes unchanged when it blocks or removes something. It must re-serialise those requests and responses. - A tool call is held for as long as the model takes to write its arguments, plus detector time. A slow judge model or webhook adds to that. - The gateway sees tool calls the model proposes. It cannot see whether a tool really ran or what it really did. Only an MCP gateway can. - The client sends the conversation history. Checks that rely on it, such as "host seen in the conversation", are hints, not proof. The gateway's own history is trusted. The client's history is not. - The design depends on Dogwood's compiled output, which may change. A pinned revision and a re-compile job limit the risk. The spike confirmed the output works with cedar-policy 4.14. Only the whitelisted temporal shapes are available to tenants. - Rules that use history lose Cedar's formal analysis tools. - Redis is now on the path of history-based rules. A Redis outage follows the fail-open or fail-closed setting. Decision events in the Redis buffer are lost if Redis is lost. - Each tenant's tool catalog must be kept up to date. A tool missing from the catalog is blocked by default. - Anthropic ingress moves forward from M2, which adds scope. ## Alternatives considered - Check in each route handler. Not chosen. LiteLLM shows that per-route enforcement leaves routes unchecked. - Hold the whole stream until it ends. Not chosen. It loses the time to the first token for every guarded request. This is what LiteLLM's tool permission guardrail does. - Fail the request on a block. Not chosen. It ends the agent turn and loses text the model already produced. - Rules in operator config only. Not chosen. Tenants could not manage their own rules. - One IAM call for each tool call. Not chosen. It adds a gRPC round trip to every tool call and puts the history far from the evaluation. - Run the Dogwood interpreter in the gateway. Not chosen. It is marked not for production, and its time grows with the history length. - Plain Cedar over a fixed set of history facts. Adopted in restricted form by the 2026-11-09 amendment of (f): the gateway evaluates a fixed set of history shapes, and tenants write them in Dogwood syntax. - A client session header. Not chosen. It needs client changes, and a client can split one session into many to escape sequence rules. - Deterministic detectors only. Not chosen. They miss fuzzy cases. The judge model is optional and can only add blocks. - A detector that blocks directly. Not chosen. All decisions go through Cedar, so one place explains every block. ## References - [SMA-747](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-747): umbrella issue, with sub-issues SMA-748 to SMA-756 - Notion "AI Gateway" scoping page, sections 6.6 and 11 - ADR-0005, ADR-0012, ADR-0013, ADR-0019, ADR-0025 - Helikon "Permissions, Guardrails & Hooks" and Helikon ADR-4 (MCP via rmcp) - AWS Dogwood: [https://github.com/dogwood-policy/dogwood](https://github.com/dogwood-policy/dogwood) and [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/opensource/introducing-dogwood-runtime-verification-for-ai-agents/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/opensource/introducing-dogwood-runtime-verification-for-ai-agents/) - AgentCore Policy GA: [https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/policy-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-generally-available/](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/policy-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-generally-available/) - Hugging Face safeagents: [https://github.com/huggingface/safeagents](https://github.com/huggingface/safeagents) - LiteLLM tool permission guardrail: [https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/guardrails/tool\_permission](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/guardrails/tool_permission) and issue [#30732](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/30732) ","cover":null,"icon":null,"full_width":false,"path":"Paigasus / Development / Architecture Decision Records","verification":{"state":"unverified"},"page_last_edited_at":"2026-11-16T22:10:31.474Z"}

toolUseResult: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"ADR-0027: Gateway tool-call interception — Cedar decisions in the gateway, Dogwood compiled in IAM, history in Redis","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/412830e8fbaa81dd8d46f14859edfb83?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/412830e8fbaa81dd8d46f14859edfb83 as of 2026-11-16T22:10:31.474Z: {"title":"ADR-0027: Gateway tool-call interception — Cedar decisions in the gateway, Dogwood compiled in IAM, history in Redis"} null Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-08 Decided by: Sven Maschek Issue: [SMA-747](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-747) Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-09-sma-749-tool-call-assembler-design.md (paigasus-core, SMA-749) Amended: 2026-11-09, decision (f), after the SMA-748 spike; 2026-11-16, decision (e), the gateway's IAM identity for the policy fetch (SMA-775), and decision (g), the longest window Builds on: ADR-0005, ADR-0012, ADR-0013, ADR-0019, ADR-0025 ## Context The gateway proxies chat requests, but it does not understand tools. It cannot see which tool the model wants to call, with which arguments, or what a tool returned. So it cannot stop an agent from calling a tool it should not call. We want two kinds of protection: - Governance. A tenant decides which tools each org, team or key may call, and with which arguments. - Defence against injected or rogue agents. A tool result can carry a prompt injection. An agent can try to send data out or escape its sandbox. Some rules need history, not one request. Example: "no outbound email after a secret was read in the same session". The Notion "AI Gateway" scoping page planned for this. Section 6.6 defines a Guardrail hook chain at the request, the response and each stream chunk. Section 11 lists two ADRs that must come first: the guardrail interface, and the canonical model including tool calls. Neither was written. The hook chain was never built. The same page has two rules this decision must change: - The v1 non-goals exclude "tool-calling routing logic". - The performance target says "streaming first-token passthrough with no added buffering". A tool call cannot be checked before its arguments are complete. We compared three existing designs (research on 2026-11-08): - LiteLLM. Python guardrail hooks, a YAML tool permission guardrail, a tool policy registry, and MCP permissions. Enforcement depends on the route. Some endpoints skip it (issues #30732 and #32201). Its tool permission guardrail buffers the whole stream. Its exact-match blocklist could be bypassed with a change of case or a trailing space. - Hugging Face safeagents. A local proxy in front of a coding agent. It streams text and holds only tool calls until they are complete. Then it allows the call or replaces it with a notice. Deterministic checks run first, then a scanner, then an optional judge model that can only add blocks. It does not inspect tool results. It trusts the conversation history that the client sends. - AWS Dogwood and AgentCore Policy. AgentCore Policy evaluates Cedar at an agent tool gateway. It is deny by default and has a log-only mode. Dogwood (open source, Apache-2.0, Rust, August 2026) extends Cedar with when temporal clauses over the history of tool calls. Its lower step turns a policy into plain Cedar plus context slots that history fills. The reference interpreter is marked not for production. It keeps history in memory, does not check timestamps, and does not log decisions. Helikon already has an in-agent design: PermissionPolicy (Allow, Deny, AskUser, Replace), Guardrail and Hook. It is not connected to the gateway. ## Decision (a) The gateway checks tool calls at one point, after it reads them into a provider-neutral model. - The first version covers OpenAI Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages. Anthropic ingress is pulled forward from M2. - Each ingress has a converter into a ToolTurn: tool definitions, tool results, and earlier tool calls. - Every rule and every detector works on this model. A new ingress gets the same checks with no rule changes. This avoids the route-dependent gaps of LiteLLM. - The original bytes are kept. When nothing changes, they are forwarded unchanged. (b) Streaming holds only tool calls. - Text frames pass through at once. The time to the first text token does not change. - When a tool call starts, its frames and all later frames are held, in order, until the call is complete. - Each held call has a byte cap and a time cap. While a call is held, the gateway sends SSE keep-alive comments. - This decision replaces the PRD rule with: text is never held; a tool call's frames are held until the call is complete. (c) A blocked tool call is replaced by an assistant notice. The request does not fail. - OpenAI: the call's deltas are dropped and a delta.content notice is sent. The remaining calls are renumbered. If every call is blocked, finish_reason becomes stop. - Anthropic: the tool_use block becomes a text block at the same index. If every call is blocked, stop_reason becomes end_turn. - The decision is also sent as an SSE comment (: paigasus-decision), or as a paigasus-tool-decisions header when not streaming. - On the request side, the gateway can remove a tool definition, or replace a tool result with a notice. It never edits the text of a tool result. (d) Cedar decides. Tenants write the policies in IAM. - Each tenant has a tool catalog in IAM. Each tool becomes a Cedar action in the action group Action::"InvokeTool". A tool that is not in the catalog is evaluated as Action::"Unregistered", so Cedar's deny-by-default blocks it. - Tool names are normalised before matching: trim, Unicode NFC, then compare case-insensitively. - The context holds the arguments (context.input), the findings of the detectors, the request, the session and the history slots. - An operator floor is a platform policy set in IAM. It may contain only forbid policies. Cedar's rule that a forbid wins over any permit means a tenant cannot loosen it. - The modes are off, log-only and enforce. A tenant starts in log-only mode with an allow-everything starter policy. - Fail-open or fail-closed is an explicit setting. (e) The gateway evaluates. IAM does not get a call for each tool call. - The decision types and decide() live in paigasus-kernel. They are synchronous and pure, so Helikon can reuse them (ADR-0005). - The gateway caches each tenant's compiled policy set. An IAM change event clears the cached copy. A periodic refresh is a backstop. The gateway has one IAM credential, for the policy fetch only. (Amended 2026-11-16, SMA-775.) - The gateway fetches a tenant's compiled set after an IAM change event or on the refresh timer. No caller is present at that time, so the fetch cannot use a caller's key. - IAM has a new system role tool_policy_reader. It holds the action ReadCompiledToolPolicies and no other action. - A dedicated gateway service account holds this role at Root. IAM has no system service accounts, so an operator makes this account by hand, in a platform organization that the operator owns, and gives it an API key. The operator runbook describes the steps. - The gateway reads the account's credential from a file (iam.service_credential_file). It reads the file again when the file changes, so a rotation needs no restart. - The gateway sends this credential only on GetCompiledToolPolicies and GetCompiledFloorPolicies. It sends it on no other RPC. - The per-request self-query does not change. IsAuthorized still carries the caller's own key and asks about the caller's own principal (SMA-446, D9). The gateway credential cannot authorize a caller's request. - Alternative not chosen: grant the read action to gateway_user. Every API-key holder could then read the compiled policies of its organization. - Risk: a leaked gateway credential exposes every tenant's compiled tool policies, but no other data. The role has one action, and the credential can be rotated without a restart. (f) Dogwood is a front end in IAM, restricted to a fixed set of history shapes. It is not an interpreter in the gateway. (Amended 2026-11-09 after the SMA-748 spike: "A-restricted".) - When a tenant saves a policy, IAM validates it with Dogwood and runs lower. Dogwood runs in its own cargo workspace or binary inside IAM, because it pins cedar-policy 4.11 and cannot join rs/. - IAM translates each temporal block into a Paigasus-owned history-condition format. Only these shapes are accepted: formerly within W, count_within W with a comparison, sum_within W with a comparison, and possibly count_distinct_within. Any other shape, or a failed lowering, rejects the save. - IAM stores the source, the compiled Cedar, the translated conditions with stable slot names (lower_with_distincter), and the pinned Dogwood revision. IAM implements @scope per policy itself, because Dogwood applies its history partitioning to the whole policy set. - The gateway evaluates the conditions from its own history store, fills the slots, and evaluates plain Cedar. It matches Dogwood's semantics: a closed window \[now−W, now\], the current request counted toward count_within, and only request events decided. A missing slot fails closed. - A Dogwood bump does not change running policies. A re-compile job must run, and it reports any differences. - Why restricted: the spike (SMA-748, 2026-11-09) found that lowered Cedar validates and evaluates under cedar-policy 4.14, and matched dogwood replay on 14 of 14 decisions. But Dogwood exports no machine-readable slot format, cannot share the workspace's Cedar version, and needs a cargo deny exception for tiny-keccak. A fixed set of shapes gives tenants Dogwood syntax on top of a gateway evaluator we own. More shapes can be added later, one at a time. (g) The gateway keeps a trusted history in Redis. - Two event kinds: call (a tool call the model proposed, with a verdict) and result (a tool result the client claims). - Only the gateway clock sets timestamps. Each event is bound to the authenticated principal. - Requests are linked into a session by the tool call ids the gateway forwarded. A policy can also read the history of the principal or the key, with @scope("principal") or @scope("key"), so a client cannot escape a rule by starting a new conversation. - A call event is written as pending before the decision and updated afterwards. Concurrent requests therefore see each other. This is the reserve-then-charge pattern of ADR-0025. - Only the argument fields that policies use are stored, plus a hash of all arguments. Tool result content is never stored. - Limits: a longest window of 24 hours, and at most 10,000 events per history. (Amended 2026-11-16: Dogwood limits every window to 24 hours, so IAM refuses a longer window. The 7-day maximum is not available.) (h) Detectors produce findings. Only Cedar decides. - Built-in detectors: undeclared tool, name collision, invalid arguments, host not seen in the conversation, secret in arguments, injection markers in tool results, and history findings (forged history, mixed sessions, truncated history). - An optional judge model runs only on suspicious calls. It sees only the system and user messages, the call and the findings. It can add a block. It can never remove one. - A signed webhook lets external providers add findings. It cannot change content. (i) Every decision is logged as an event. - A new ToolDecisionEvent proto embeds AuditMetadata (ADR-0012). It holds no raw arguments or content. - Events go into a Redis stream first and are published to NATS JetStream. - A CLI exports the log in Dogwood's trace format, so a tenant can test a policy with dogwood replay before enforcing it. - New error codes go in a gateway block of error.proto (ADR-0019). (j) An MCP gateway is a later phase. It reuses the same action, history and decision log (SMA-756). ## Consequences Positive - One check point covers every ingress, so a new endpoint cannot skip the checks. - Text streaming keeps its latency. Only tool calls wait. - Tenants write policies in Cedar, which the platform already uses, and can use Dogwood sequence rules. - The not-for-production Dogwood interpreter never runs on live traffic. - Helikon can reuse the decision shape, so the agent side and the gateway side can enforce the same policy. - Log-only mode and trace replay let a tenant test a policy before it blocks anything. Negative and risks - The gateway no longer forwards bytes unchanged when it blocks or removes something. It must re-serialise those requests and responses. - A tool call is held for as long as the model takes to write its arguments, plus detector time. A slow judge model or webhook adds to that. - The gateway sees tool calls the model proposes. It cannot see whether a tool really ran or what it really did. Only an MCP gateway can. - The client sends the conversation history. Checks that rely on it, such as "host seen in the conversation", are hints, not proof. The gateway's own history is trusted. The client's history is not. - The design depends on Dogwood's compiled output, which may change. A pinned revision and a re-compile job limit the risk. The spike confirmed the output works with cedar-policy 4.14. Only the whitelisted temporal shapes are available to tenants. - Rules that use history lose Cedar's formal analysis tools. - Redis is now on the path of history-based rules. A Redis outage follows the fail-open or fail-closed setting. Decision events in the Redis buffer are lost if Redis is lost. - Each tenant's tool catalog must be kept up to date. A tool missing from the catalog is blocked by default. - Anthropic ingress moves forward from M2, which adds scope. ## Alternatives considered - Check in each route handler. Not chosen. LiteLLM shows that per-route enforcement leaves routes unchecked. - Hold the whole stream until it ends. Not chosen. It loses the time to the first token for every guarded request. This is what LiteLLM's tool permission guardrail does. - Fail the request on a block. Not chosen. It ends the agent turn and loses text the model already produced. - Rules in operator config only. Not chosen. Tenants could not manage their own rules. - One IAM call for each tool call. Not chosen. It adds a gRPC round trip to every tool call and puts the history far from the evaluation. - Run the Dogwood interpreter in the gateway. Not chosen. It is marked not for production, and its time grows with the history length. - Plain Cedar over a fixed set of history facts. Adopted in restricted form by the 2026-11-09 amendment of (f): the gateway evaluates a fixed set of history shapes, and tenants write them in Dogwood syntax. - A client session header. Not chosen. It needs client changes, and a client can split one session into many to escape sequence rules. - Deterministic detectors only. Not chosen. They miss fuzzy cases. The judge model is optional and can only add blocks. - A detector that blocks directly. Not chosen. All decisions go through Cedar, so one place explains every block. ## References - [SMA-747](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-747): umbrella issue, with sub-issues SMA-748 to SMA-756 - Notion "AI Gateway" scoping page, sections 6.6 and 11 - ADR-0005, ADR-0012, ADR-0013, ADR-0019, ADR-0025 - Helikon "Permissions, Guardrails & Hooks" and Helikon ADR-4 (MCP via rmcp) - AWS Dogwood: [https://github.com/dogwood-policy/dogwood](https://github.com/dogwood-policy/dogwood) and [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/opensource/introducing-dogwood-runtime-verification-for-ai-agents/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/opensource/introducing-dogwood-runtime-verification-for-ai-agents/) - AgentCore Policy GA: [https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/policy-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-generally-available/](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/03/policy-amazon-bedrock-agentcore-generally-available/) - Hugging Face safeagents: [https://github.com/huggingface/safeagents](https://github.com/huggingface/safeagents) - LiteLLM tool permission guardrail: [https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/guardrails/tool\_permission](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/guardrails/tool_permission) and issue [#30732](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/30732) ","cover":null,"icon":null,"full_width":false,"path":"Paigasus / Development / Architecture Decision Records","verification":{"state":"unverified"},"page_last_edited_at":"2026-11-16T22:10:31.474Z"}

content.content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"Library + pluggable Runner trait; durability is a seam, not built-in","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/355830e8fbaa81a483dafbf8a9cfcc15?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/355830e8fbaa81a483dafbf8a9cfcc15 as of 2026-05-15T19:18:41.379Z: {"ADR ID":"ADR-6","Area":["Runtime"],"Drivers":"Production teams will need ephemeral, durable, and AWS-managed execution; we cannot pick one.","Status":"Accepted","Title":"Library + pluggable Runner trait; durability is a seam, not built-in","date:Date:is_datetime":0,"date:Date:start":"2026-05-03","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/355830e8fbaa81a483dafbf8a9cfcc15"} null ## Context Production agent deployments fall into three shapes: ephemeral tokio process, Temporal-style durable execution, and AWS Bedrock AgentCore (per-session microVM with up to 8h duration). Hard-coding any one of them into the SDK loses the others. ## Decision The SDK is a library. The agent loop's execution backend is the Runner trait: ```rs #[async_trait::async_trait] pub trait Runner: Send + Sync { async fn run>( &self, agent: &A, ctx: RunContext, input: AgentInput, config: RunConfig, ) -> Result; } ``` Three implementations live in separate crates: - paigasus-helikon-runtime-tokio — default ephemeral. - paigasus-helikon-runtime-temporal — wraps each Tool::invoke in a Temporal Activity; loop becomes a Workflow. - paigasus-helikon-runtime-agentcore — implements the AgentCore container protocol (port 8080 /invocations, SSE responses, port 8000 MCP). ## Consequences - Users opt in via Cargo features. - Rust binaries (10–30MB, \<50ms cold start) are an excellent fit for the AgentCore microVM model. - A paigasus-helikon-runtime-axum companion crate ships REST/SSE/WebSocket for self-hosted deployment. ## Caveat Temporal's Rust SDK is alpha. Pragmatic short-term: a Python orchestration tier calling a Rust agent service over HTTP/MCP. The SQLite table definition for this page's parent data source. content.content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"ADR-0006: Open-core boundary as a published-artifact dependency edge","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/368830e8fbaa81fa9d11cbf049ff986d?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/368830e8fbaa81fa9d11cbf049ff986d as of 2026-05-22T17:39:24.511Z: {"title":"ADR-0006: Open-core boundary as a published-artifact dependency edge"} null Status: Accepted Date: 2026-05-22 Deciders: Sven ## Context Paigasus is open-core. paigasus-core is the public OSS repo (Apache 2.0, see ADR-0007); paigasus-cloud is private and proprietary. The boundary between them needs to be clean. Leaks from cloud to public are reputation-damaging. A fuzzy boundary creates ongoing maintenance friction. The instinctive option — a monorepo with feature flags, or git-filter-branch extraction tricks — creates leak risk and ongoing maintenance friction. ## Decision Enforce the open-core boundary as a published-artifact dependency edge. paigasus-cloud consumes published versions of paigasus-kernel, paigasus-proto, etc., from [crates.io](http://crates.io) / PyPI / npm. No git submodules. No symlinks. No build-flag gating. No code-extraction tricks. For pre-release coordination (cloud consuming RC versions of unreleased core), mirror through AWS CodeArtifact (already in use). CodeArtifact's upstream-mirror behavior means cloud's CI resolves transparently — RC from internal CodeArtifact, stable from public registries, no manifest changes between phases. ## Rationale - Forces a clean, stable, semver-enforced API between the core and commercial halves. Same discipline as a well-designed library boundary. - Lockfiles in cloud become auditable. Any git+https dep or path dep is an immediate leak signal. - Eliminates the "is this code public-leaning or private-leaning" judgment from every PR. The answer is which repo it's in. - Plays well with the CLA (ADR-0007). With a CLA in place, any public-side contribution can flow into cloud through the published-artifact channel without per-contributor permission. ## Consequences Positive: - Zero leak risk from accidental file inclusion. The boundary is enforced at the dependency layer. - Clean release pipeline. Cloud can pin specific public versions for stability and upgrade deliberately. - API discipline. Any public-side change that cloud depends on requires a proper release. Public-side refactors that change the published surface become visible and reviewable. Negative (accepted): - Cloud can't urgently fix a core bug without releasing core first. Mitigated by RC publishing through CodeArtifact for fast internal iteration. - Public-side API design pressure increases since cloud is a real consumer. Mostly positive (forces clean APIs) but can slow down public-side refactors that touch the public surface. ## Alternatives considered ### Monorepo with feature flags (e.g., #[cfg(feature = "cloud")]) Rejected because: leaks proprietary feature existence and shape even when the code is gated. Mixes maintenance models. Makes "is this public?" a question that has to be answered per-file. The cost compounds as the codebase grows. ### Git submodules Rejected because: operationally fragile, fork-prone, awkward in CI. Versioned package deps are strictly better in every dimension. ### git-filter-branch / sparse-checkout extraction Rejected because: maintenance nightmare. One mistake leaks proprietary history. The dependency-edge approach achieves the same separation with mature, off-the-shelf tooling. ## Revisit triggers - If managing cloud-vs-core release coordination becomes a recurring source of friction in practice. - If the artifact-publishing pipeline becomes unreliable enough that direct path deps would be more stable. - If Paigasus's open-core model is abandoned (full OSS or full proprietary), this decision is moot. ## References - [Polyglot Monorepo Scoping](https://www.notion.so/368830e8fbaa8101b0ffded7a3de3b53) § 4 — open-core boundary mechanics, CodeArtifact RC flow, release pipeline. - [ADR-0007](https://www.notion.so/368830e8fbaa81f2a86fe3588088211f) — Apache 2.0 + CLA, the licensing posture that operates on the public side of this boundary. - [ADR-0005](https://www.notion.so/368830e8fbaa817e8184d8f22f4d487c) — the kernel + FFI bindings that are the primary published artifacts crossing this boundary. ","cover":null,"icon":null,"full_width":false,"path":"Paigasus / Development / Architecture Decision Records","verification":{"state":"unverified"},"page_last_edited_at":"2026-05-22T17:39:24.511Z"}

content.content: {"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"📡 ADR-0016: NATS JetStream as the event broker for Paigasus IAM","url":"https://app.notion.com/p/3b5830e8fbaa818aab42f372cad9b3c8?pvs=204","text":"Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3b5830e8fbaa818aab42f372cad9b3c8 as of 2026-09-01T15:33:43.037Z: {"title":"ADR-0016: NATS JetStream as the event broker for Paigasus IAM"} {"type":"emoji","emoji":"📡"} Status — accepted (amended 2026-09-01 · SMA-606: tenancy event types, 8 subjects → 22; PII posture restated) Date — 2026-08-07 (accepted 2026-08-10) Context Paigasus IAM has a complete transactional outbox and nothing at the end of it. Rows are written in the triggering mutation's own transaction (PgOutbox::enqueue), a FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED relay drains them with per-row attempt counting and poison parking, retention and a dead-letter inspect/replay surface landed with [SMA-469](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-469), and the whole path is instrumented. But the only production EventPublisher is TracingEventPublisher, which emits a tracing::info! and returns Ok(()). No process outside paigasus-iam can react to an IAM event. Closing that gap ([SMA-471](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-471)) means picking a broker, which is a first for paigasus-core — there is no message infrastructure of any kind in the repo today, and no deployment artifacts at all. Two requirements shaped the choice: consumers will be both internal and external (so the envelope is a public contract, not an internal detail), and latency matters (so a durable log with real fan-out, not a queue polled on a cron). Full design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-07-sma-471-broker-event-publisher-design.md in paigasus-core. Decision 1. NATS with JetStream is the broker, via the official async-nats Rust client. A single static Go binary, durable file-backed streams, independent consumer positions, sub-millisecond fan-out, and cheap to run both locally (nats-server -js) and in a per-test container. 2. Server-side deduplication via Nats-Msg-Id. Every publish carries the outbox row's UUID as the message id; JetStream's per-stream duplicate_window collapses a redelivery and acks it as a duplicate, which the publisher treats as success. This is the property that made JetStream win over Redis Streams — it is the difference between the relay's at-least-once retries being safe in the common case and being visible to every consumer. 3. Publishes are ack-waited. send_publish returns a future; awaiting it is what waits for persistence. Only a persisted ack becomes Ok(()), because the relay stamps published_at on Ok and never revisits the row — returning early would silently lose events. 4. CloudEvents 1.0, JSON, structured content mode is the wire envelope. id/source/type/subject/time map onto the existing DomainEvent fields; schemaversion, actorprn and correlationid are extension attributes; the outbox's free-form payload passes through as data untouched. The envelope is under contract; the per-event-type payload schemas are not. 5. Subject is the EventType wire string verbatim — iam.principal.created, iam.role.revoked, and the six others. Those strings are already stable by contract, so the subject space needs no new invention. Stream IAM_EVENTS filters iam.>. Environment separation is a NATS account/domain concern, deliberately not a subject prefix. 6. The stream is ensured at boot and its live config verified. get_or_create_stream creates or adopts; it does not reconcile. Adoption is therefore conditional: a stream whose duplicate_window, storage type, subjects or max_age are weaker than configured fails startup rather than being silently accepted. 7. The backend is config-selected and defaults to tracing. [outbox.publisher].backend = "tracing" | "nats", mirroring how authn.jwks_cache and authz.cache default to memory with redis opt-in. Nats-Msg-Id covers the common case (a lost ack retried on the next tick). It does not cover a relay tick that published and then failed to commit (the relay does a whole batch on one transaction, so a crash rolls back the bookkeeping but not the publishes), nor a crash-restart, nor an operator dead-letter replay hours later. Consumers must be idempotent. Closing the remaining gap means committing published_at per row rather than per batch, which is deferred. - Dead-letter replay republishes the same event id, arbitrarily later, and is therefore outside any sane dedup window. Minting a fresh id was rejected — it would change the consumer's dedup key for the same logical event, trading a detectable duplicate for an undetectable one — and refusing late replays was rejected because it removes the operator's only recovery tool. The exposure is instead surfaced (parked age in the list response) and measured (a beyond_dedup_window label on the replay counter). - CloudEvents scopes event identity to (source, id); JetStream keys on id alone. The resolution: consumers dedup on id, and source MUST stay stable for the lifetime of a stream. Changing source on a live stream is a breaking operational act. - iam.> carries the full authorization change graph. The payloads are secret-free and PII-free (audited: principal ids and kinds, api-key ids and display prefixes, grant ids and role keys — no email, no hash, no token material), but with subject = aggregate_prn and the actorprn extension a subscriber sees who granted whom which role on which org, in real time. Subject-level NATS permissions are a deployment requirement, not an optimization. [SMA-493](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-493) discharged that requirement: a dedicated account with least-privilege per-identity grants is provisioned by ops/nats/provision.sh and proven by repo:nats-permissions, a CI gate that boots a real broker with the committed permission config and asserts the grants are sufficient and not broader — every route to the change graph (sub iam.>, a self-created wider consumer, STREAM.MSG.GET, DIRECT.GET, and another identity's reply inbox) is asserted denied, on the server's own permissions-violation message rather than on a timeout. - A new operational dependency, and the service needs stream read and create permission on NATS, not merely publish. Two further grants proved non-obvious in SMA-493. A JetStream publisher also needs subscribe on its own inbox — the persistence ack returns there, so without it every publish times out; it is never literally write-only. And a pull consumer's subject filter cannot be enforced with subscribe permissions at all, because pull deliveries land on the requester's inbox rather than on iam.*. The filter lives in a pre-provisioned durable, and denying every form of CONSUMER.CREATE — including on the consumer's own durable name — is what makes it binding. - Environment separation is an account, and that account is now specified. PAIGASUS_IAM holds all IAM event traffic with explicit JetStream limits, separate from SYS. Both service identities live inside it: a cross-account split would require JetStream service exports/imports for the consumer API and buys no isolation the per-identity grants do not already provide, since the boundary that matters is IAM events vs. every other tenant of the broker. A third identity, iam-provisioner, is operator tooling and is deployed nowhere — it is deliberately the one full reader. - Credentials are re-read on every connection attempt. SMA-471 left open whether async-nats re-reads .creds on reconnect. It does not: with_credentials_file reads inside the options constructor and caches the JWT for the life of the client, so a rotated file is never seen and an expiring user JWT strands a long-running process — it survives until its next reconnect and then cannot authenticate. SMA-493 replaced it with with_auth_callback, which async-nats invokes on every connection attempt, so rotation needs no restart; the TLS root bundle is rebuilt per attempt too, giving CA rotation the same property. Note the subtlety this hid: a test that reconnects by constructing a new client cannot detect the defect, because fresh options re-read the file under either implementation. - TLS and credential posture are enforced at boot rather than documented. A nats backend now requires tls:// and a credentials_file, and rejects url-embedded credentials unconditionally — async-nats ignores url userinfo entirely, so a config carrying REDACTED connects anonymously while appearing authenticated. A single flag waives the transport and credential requirements together for dev and CI. Naming a CA bundle also replaces the system trust store rather than extending it, which makes a later move to a publicly-trusted broker certificate a total outage unless the bundle is updated. - Still missing after SMA-493: there is no account-JWT revocation story and no operator or account key rotation — SMA-493 rotates user credentials only. Nothing alerts on an approaching credential expiry either, though provision.sh mints non-expiring user JWTs, so the outage that motivated the rotation work requires an operator to opt into expiry. - A single-node File stream ack is weaker durability than "persisted" suggests — fsync cadence is server-configured, so an unclean node crash can lose an acked message while the outbox row is already marked published. Production wants sync_interval: always or num_replicas: 3. - Latency is not yet improved by this decision. Delivery remains gated by the relay's poll interval (5 s default); the post-commit nudge that would fix it is deferred. The requirement drove the choice of broker, not yet the delivery path. - Because publishes can now fail, outbox.max_attempts was raised 5 → 60: at a 5 s poll interval the old default dead-lettered the entire in-flight backlog after a 25-second broker restart. Alternatives considered - Redis Streams — zero new infrastructure, since redis is already a workspace dependency. Rejected: Redis is a weak durable log. XADD MAXLEN trims by count or size with no retention-by-age guarantee, consumer-group bookkeeping (pending-entry lists, claim/ack) would be ours to operate, and there is no server-side publish deduplication — every property Decision 2 depends on would have been hand-built and hand-tested. - Kafka / Redpanda — the strongest ecosystem for external subscribers and the best long-retention story. Rejected on operational weight: a broker plus its coordination is a large first infrastructure dependency for today's event volume, and it is slow to stand up per integration test. Worth revisiting if external subscriber demand or volume grows by an order of magnitude. - Managed cloud brokers (GCP Pub/Sub, AWS SNS+SQS, Azure Service Bus) — no infrastructure to run. Rejected: binds paigasus-core, a public and self-hostable Apache-2.0 repo, to a single cloud, and forces local development and CI onto an emulator. Contradicts the repo's posture (ADR-0003). - Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY — tempting because the outbox is already in Postgres. Rejected outright: no durability for a disconnected consumer, an 8 kB payload cap, and no fan-out with independent positions. - A bespoke JSON envelope mirroring the outbox row one-to-one — least code. Rejected: a contract we would have to invent, document and defend to external consumers, for no gain over a standard that already fits the data. - Protobuf via contracts/ — would match ADR-0004's proto-first posture and put the event schema behind the existing buf breaking gate. Rejected for scope: payload is free-form serde_json::Value today, so this means eight typed payload messages and a change to how the outbox is written. Not foreclosed — CloudEvents has a protobuf format, so this remains the natural upgrade path when typed payloads are needed. ## Amendment — 2026-09-01 (SMA-606) SMA-606 adds the tenancy audit-log and domain-event trail — an AuditEntry and a DomainEvent on every organization, team, project and membership mutation. Two things in this ADR change. ### 1. Decision 5 — the subject space grows from 8 to 22 Decision 5 fixes the subject as the EventType wire string verbatim and enumerates it as "iam.principal.created, iam.role.revoked, and the six others". SMA-606 adds fourteen: iam.{organization,team,project}.{created,renamed,archived,restored} and iam.membership.{attached,detached}. The rule is unchanged — the subject is still the wire string verbatim, still under iam.> — so stream IAM_EVENTS's filter and iam-publisher's iam.> publish grant need no edit. Only the enumeration is now out of date, and this amendment is the correction. ops/nats/permissions.md §3's reasoning about why a subject filter cannot live in a permission is likewise unaffected; it now simply covers a wider space. One existing consumer is affected, and it is worth naming. iam.role.granted acquires a third emitter. RoleService::grant and BootstrapAdminSeeder::seed_grant already emit it; organization create now does too, for the org_admin owner grant it writes in the same transaction. Because iam.role.granted is one of the six CONSUMER_FILTER_SUBJECTS the gateway-cache-invalidator durable filters on, every organization create now delivers a message to that durable. That is wanted — a new org_admin grant genuinely changes authorization decisions, which is why the subject is filtered in the first place — but it is throughput SMA-492 did not size for. The event carries "source": "organization_create" in its payload so a future consumer can distinguish it from a user-requested grant, following the convention BootstrapAdminSeeder established with "source": "bootstrap_admins". ### 2. The "PII-free" consequence needs a narrower statement The consequence beginning "iam.> carries the full authorization change graph" audits the payloads as "secret-free and PII-free (audited: principal ids and kinds, api-key ids and display prefixes, grant ids and role keys — no email, no hash, no token material)". That audit was exhaustive over the eight event types that existed when it was written. The tenancy payloads add two fields that are not identifiers: slug and name. slug is constrained by Slug::parse. name is operator-controlled free text, and nothing constrains its content. So the accurate statement is no longer "the payloads are PII-free" but: > The payloads carry no PII by construction except a tenancy node's name, which is whatever an operator typed. This changes no decision in this ADR. It changes what a reader may assume. An operator who puts a person's name in an organization name has put it on iam.> and into audit_log.detail. The exposure is bounded by the permissions SMA-493 provisioned — only iam-provisioner may subscribe to iam.>, and the audit read path is Root-only — but it is now bounded by permission rather than by construction, and that distinction belongs in the document that made the original claim. The secret-free half of the audit is unaffected: no tenancy payload carries a hash, a token, or any credential material. io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo.description: Notion's official MCP server lets you use your Notion workspace as a system of record for knowledge work and software development. Search questions about the codebase and business, fetch links to pages such as tech specs and PRDs, and track tasks with your team.

## 1. ADR location, schema, list, next number

- The ADR container is a PAGE, not a database. It has no data source ID and no properties except the title.
  - Title: "Architecture Decision Records". ID `368830e8-fbaa-816c-b411-c7ee1682c175`.
  - URL: https://app.notion.com/p/368830e8fbaa816cb411c7ee1682c175
  - Path: Paigasus / Development.
  - Each ADR is a sub-page. A hand-maintained Index table sits on the parent page: `# | Title | Status | Date`. The rows are page mentions. A new ADR needs a new row there.
- Page-body format rules, quoted in summary:
  - Title pattern `ADR-NNNN: Decision summary` (zero-padded).
  - Body fields, in this order: Status, Date ("when the decision was accepted"), Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives considered.
  - Status values: `proposed` / `accepted` / `superseded by ADR-XXXX` / `deprecated`.
  - Superseded ADRs are never deleted. The page says the style is "lightweight MADR-style".
  - It also defines "ADR vs guideline": an ADR needs viable alternatives.
- All 27 ADRs have status Accepted. I saw no Proposed, Superseded or Rejected entry. Dates are in brackets.
  - 0001 axum over actix-web (05-22)
  - 0002 basedpyright (05-22)
  - 0003 one public polyglot monorepo plus private cloud repo (05-22)
  - 0004 protobuf + buf for wire contracts (05-22)
  - 0005 shared logic in Rust `paigasus-kernel`, bound to Py/Node/WASM (05-22)
  - 0006 open-core boundary as a published-artifact dependency edge (05-22)
  - 0007 Apache 2.0 + CLA + trademark (05-22)
  - 0008 Moon (05-22)
  - 0009 ESLint+Prettier (05-22)

  - 0012 cross-language shared data shapes via embedded proto messages (06-21)
  - 0013 Cedar for authorization (06-21)
  - 0014 tenancy and PRN (06-21)
  - 0015 Authenticator port and OIDC (07-06)
  - 0016 NATS JetStream event broker for IAM (08-07)
  - 0017 console topology and session ownership (08-13)
  - 0018 Connect-ES over gRPC (08-13)
  - 0019 canonical error model, `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` (08-13)
  - 0020 service capability discovery (08-13)
  - 0021 Tailwind + Radix (08-13)
  - 0022 TS consumers of the kernel use the wasm binding (09-22)
  - 0023 interactive-user auth on the gateway chat surface (09-23)
  - 0024 operator-attested external identity linking (09-27)

  - 0026 gateway accepts DPoP-bound tokens (10-04)
  - 0027 gateway tool-call interception: Cedar, Dogwood, Redis history (11-08)
- **Next free number: ADR-0028.** The index ends at 0027. I did not scan for unlisted child pages.
- A separate Helikon ADR database exists. It is "Decisions (ADRs)" under Paigasus / Agents / Paigasus Helikon - AI SDK.
  - Database URL: https://app.notion.com/p/c3b212ed0c734f0ca3052ecb961a0e0e
  - Data source: `collection://7078dae0-4eda-49c1-91df-2ef721ae2ec6`.
  - Properties: Status (Proposed/Accepted/Superseded/Rejected/Deprecated), Drivers, Date, "ADR ID" (read-only integer, shown as `ADR-6`), Area (multi-select: Tools, Model Provider, Sessions, Multi-Agent, Runtime, Observability, Permissions & Guardrails, MCP, Tooling & Macros, Errors), Title.
